sections.heading: What measurement means
paragraphs: Chemistry is built on measured amounts. A measurement has two parts: a number and a unit. The number alone is not enough. Saying "the sample is 5" does not tell you whether that is 5 grams, 5 milliliters, or 5 moles.
A unit is the agreed scale you used. Grams measure mass. Liters measure volume. Seconds measure time. Kelvin measures temperature on the absolute scale used in science.

Scientists use SI units so results can be compared across labs. The SI base units you will meet first are the kilogram (kg) for mass, the meter (m) for length, and the second (s) for time. In chemistry we often use related units that are more handy at the bench: the gram (g), the liter (L), and the milliliter (mL).

Prefixes scale a unit up or down by powers of ten. kilo (k) means 10³, so 1 kg = 1000 g. centi (c) means 10⁻², so 1 cm = 0.01 m. milli (m) means 10⁻³, so 1 mL = 0.001 L. micro (µ) means 10⁻⁶. nano (n) means 10⁻⁹.
Why prefixes exist: writing 0.000001 g is easy to miscount. Writing 1 µg keeps the digit count small and the meaning clear.
sections.why: Every lab number you report must carry a unit. Without the unit, the next student or instrument cannot use your result.

sections.heading: Dimensional analysis (unit conversion)
paragraphs: Dimensional analysis is a method for converting one unit into another by multiplying by conversion factors. A conversion factor is a fraction equal to 1, built from a true equality of units.

Example of a true equality: 1 kg = 1000 g. From that you can write two fractions that both equal 1: (1 kg)/(1000 g) and (1000 g)/(1 kg). You choose the fraction that cancels the unit you want to remove.

Units cancel the same way numbers cancel in a fraction. If grams appear on top and bottom, those grams cancel. What remains is the unit you want. That is why the method is reliable: a wrong conversion factor leaves the wrong unit in the answer, so you can catch the mistake before you finish.

worked.title: Convert 2.50 kg to grams
steps: Write what you start with, including the unit: 2.50 kg.
Write the equality that links kg and g: 1 kg = 1000 g.
Build the conversion factor that puts kg on the bottom so kg will cancel: (1000 g)/(1 kg).
Cancel the kg unit on top with the kg unit on the bottom.
The remaining unit is g. So the exact product is 2500 g.
Check significant figures. 2.50 has 3 significant figures. 1000 in this equality is an exact defined count (kilo means exactly 1000), so it does not limit sig figs.
Report 2.50 × 10³ g, or 2500 g with a clear note that 3 sig figs apply. Prefer scientific notation when trailing zeros would be unclear: 2.50 × 10³ g.

workedExamples.title: Convert 375 mL to liters
steps: Choose the factor with mL on the bottom: (1 L)/(1000 mL).
Unit left: L. Result so far: 0.375 L.
Sig figs: 375 has 3 significant figures (leading zeros after a decimal would not count, but here the digits are 3, 7, 5). The 1000 mL per L is exact.

sections.heading: Significant figures
paragraphs: Significant figures (sig figs) are the digits in a measured value that are known with confidence, plus one estimated digit. They tell the reader how precise the measurement was.
Why they matter: if a balance only reads to 0.01 g, writing 12.3444 g pretends you know more than the instrument can show. Sig figs stop you from inventing precision.
Counting rules for a written number:
1. Non-zero digits (1 to 9) are always significant. Example: 23.4 has 3 sig figs.
2. Zeros between non-zero digits are significant. Example: 1002 has 4 sig figs.
3. Leading zeros (zeros before the first non-zero digit) are not significant. They only place the decimal. Example: 0.00456 has 3 sig figs (4, 5, 6).
4. Trailing zeros after a decimal point are significant. Example: 12.30 has 4 sig figs. The final zero means the tenths place was measured as zero, not left blank.

5. Trailing zeros in a whole number with no decimal point are ambiguous. 1500 might have 2, 3, or 4 sig figs. Avoid the ambiguity by writing scientific notation: 1.5 × 10³ (2 sig figs) or 1.500 × 10³ (4 sig figs).

worked.title: How many sig figs in 0.02050?
steps: Leading zeros before 2 are not significant. Drop 0.0 from the count.
The zero between 2 and 5 is between non-zero digits, so it counts.
The trailing zero after the decimal (the last 0) counts because it sits after the decimal point.

sections.heading: Sig figs when you calculate
paragraphs: Multiplication and division use one rule. Addition and subtraction use a different rule. Mixing the two rules is a common source of wrong answers.

Multiplication and division: the result may have only as many significant figures as the factor with the fewest significant figures. Why: each measured factor contributes uncertainty, and the weakest link sets the limit.

Addition and subtraction: look at decimal places, not at the count of sig figs. The result may have only as many digits after the decimal as the addend with the fewest digits after the decimal. Why: you cannot know a hundredths place if one of the numbers only went to tenths.

worked.title: Multiply 4.56 g × 1.4 (density-style product)
steps: Count sig figs in 4.56: 3 sig figs.
Count sig figs in 1.4: 2 sig figs.
The tighter limit is 2 sig figs.
Round 6.384 to 2 sig figs. Look at the first two digits: 6 and 3. The next digit is 8, which is 5 or greater, so round the 3 up to 4.
2 sig figs for a number between 1 and 10 means one digit before the decimal and one after when written plainly, but 6.4 already has 2 sig figs.
Final answer: 6.4 (with whatever unit the product carries).

workedExamples.title: Add 12.11 mL + 0.3 mL + 1.007 mL
steps: Look at decimal places, not total sig figs.
The strictest limit is 1 digit after the decimal (from 0.3).
Round 13.417 so only 1 digit remains after the decimal. The tenths digit is 4. The next digit is 1, which is less than 5, so the 4 stays.

mistake.wrong: Common mistake: treating 12.00 g + 1.1 g like a multiplication problem and cutting the answer to 2 sig figs as 13 g.
mistake.whyWrong: Addition is limited by decimal places, not by the sig-fig count. 12.00 is known to the hundredths place. 1.1 is known only to the tenths place. The sum must stop at tenths, which gives 13.1 g, not a 2-sig-fig chop to 13 g.
mistake.correct: Correct way: 12.00 + 1.1 = 13.10 raw, then round to one digit after the decimal because of 1.1. Answer: 13.1 g.

sections.heading: Density
paragraphs: Density is mass per unit volume. As a formula: density ρ = m / V. If mass is in grams and volume is in milliliters, density has units g/mL. For solids you will also see g/cm³. 1 mL = 1 cm³ by definition, so g/mL and g/cm³ match for this purpose.

Why density is useful: it lets you convert between mass and volume for a pure substance when you know one of them. Water near room temperature has a density of about 1.00 g/mL. That is a standard value you may use unless a problem gives a different temperature value.
Rearrangements you will need: m = ρ × V, and V = m / ρ. Always write the units in the setup so they cancel to the unit you want.

worked.title: Mass of 25.0 mL of a liquid with density 0.789 g/mL
steps: Write the given volume: V = 25.0 mL.
Write the given density: ρ = 0.789 g/mL.
Choose the form that solves for mass: m = ρ × V.
Substitute with units: m = 0.789 g/mL × 25.0 mL.
Cancel mL on top and bottom.
0.789 × 25 = 19.725; keep the extra place for now: 19.725.
Sig figs for multiplication: 0.789 has 3 sig figs; 25.0 has 3 sig figs. Limit = 3 sig figs.
Round 19.725 to 3 sig figs. Digits: 1, 9, 7. Next digit is 2, so do not round up.

workedExamples.title: Volume of 40.0 g of a metal with density 8.96 g/cm³
steps: Solve for volume: V = m / ρ.
Sig figs: 40.0 has 3; 8.96 has 3. Limit = 3 sig figs.

sections.heading: Check yourself
paragraphs: Pause here and try these without looking up. Then read the answers.

items.q: How many significant figures are in 0.06030?
items.a: 4 (6, 0, 3, 0). Leading zeros do not count. The trailing zero after the decimal does count.
2.00 × 10³ g (or 2000 g with 3 sig figs stated). Use 1 kg = 1000 g and cancel kg.

items.q: A cube of metal has mass 54.0 g and volume 20.0 cm³. What is its density?
items.a: ρ = 54.0 g / 20.0 cm³ = 2.70 g/cm³ (3 sig figs from both inputs).

sections.heading: Atoms and isotopes
paragraphs: An atom has protons (Z, atomic number) and neutrons in the nucleus, with electrons outside. Mass number A = protons + neutrons. Isotopes of an element share Z but differ in neutrons.
For an ion, charge = protons − electrons. Example: ⁵⁶Fe³⁺ has Z = 26, so 26 protons, A − Z = 30 neutrons, and 26 − 3 = 23 electrons.

figure.alt: Diagram of an iron-56 Fe3+ ion: nucleus with 26 protons and 30 neutrons, and an electron cloud with 23 electrons after losing three.

sections.heading: Average atomic mass
paragraphs: The periodic-table atomic mass is a weighted average of isotope masses: Σ (fraction × mass).

worked.title: Average atomic mass of Cl
steps: Isotopes: 75.78% ³⁵Cl (34.969 u) and 24.22% ³⁷Cl (36.966 u)

sections.heading: The mole
paragraphs: One mole contains Avogadro's number N_A ≈ 6.022 × 10²³ particles. Molar mass M (g/mol) equals the formula mass in u. n = m / M converts grams to moles.

worked.title: Moles of water in 10.0 g H₂O

sections.heading: Formulas and percent composition
paragraphs: An empirical formula is the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms. A molecular formula is a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula. Mass percent of an element = (mass of element in 1 mol of compound / molar mass) × 100%.

worked.title: Mass % N in NH₄NO₃
steps: Mass of N in 1 mol = 2 × 14.01 = 28.02 g

sections.heading: Empirical formula from % composition
paragraphs: Assume 100 g of sample so % becomes grams. Convert each element to moles, divide by the smallest mole amount, and scale to whole numbers.

sections.heading: Molecular formula and oxidation states
paragraphs: If molar mass / empirical-formula mass = n, multiply subscripts by n. Example: CH₂O with M = 180 g/mol → n = 180/30 = 6 → C₆H₁₂O₆.
Oxidation state (oxidation number) is a bookkeeping charge: O is usually −2, H is +1 with nonmetals, elemental form is 0, and the sum equals the ion or molecule charge.

sections.heading: Chemical equations and why we balance them
paragraphs: A chemical equation is a compact sentence that shows reactants turning into products. Reactants are written on the left. Products are written on the right. An arrow points from reactants to products.
Example skeleton: H₂ + O₂ → H₂O. This is not yet ready to use for amounts, because it is not balanced.

Balanced means each element has the same number of atoms on both sides. Why we balance: atoms are not created or destroyed in ordinary chemical change (conservation of mass). A balanced equation is the bookkeeping that respects that rule.

Coefficients are the numbers placed in front of formulas. They scale the whole formula. In 2 H₂O the coefficient 2 means two water molecules (or two moles of water). Subscripts inside a formula are part of the identity of the substance. You may change coefficients when balancing. You must not change subscripts, or you invent a different compound.
States of matter in parentheses are optional helpers: (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas, (aq) dissolved in water. They do not change the atom count.

worked.title: Balance H₂ + O₂ → H₂O
steps: Count atoms on the left: H = 2, O = 2.
Count atoms on the right: H = 2, O = 1.
Oxygen is short on the right. Place coefficient 2 in front of H₂O: H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O.
Recount the right side: H = 4, O = 2.
Hydrogen on the left is now short (only 2). Place coefficient 2 in front of H₂: 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O.
Recount left: H = 4, O = 2. Right: H = 4, O = 2.
Both sides match. The balanced equation is 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O.
Read it in moles when you do stoichiometry: 2 mol H₂ react with 1 mol O₂ to make 2 mol H₂O.

sections.why: A balanced equation gives the mole ratios you need for every later stoichiometry step. An unbalanced equation gives false ratios.

sections.heading: Mole ratios from the balanced equation
paragraphs: The mole (mol) is the chemist's counting unit for particles. One mole of any substance contains 6.022 × 10²³ particles (Avogadro's number). For stoichiometry you mostly need this idea: a balanced equation's coefficients are mole ratios.
From 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O you may write ratios such as (2 mol H₂)/(1 mol O₂) or (2 mol H₂O)/(2 mol H₂). Each of those fractions equals 1 in the sense of a conversion factor between the linked amounts.

Molar mass converts grams to moles and moles to grams. Molar mass is the mass of one mole of a substance in g/mol. You build it from atomic molar masses on the periodic table. Standard values we use here: H = 1.008 g/mol, C = 12.01 g/mol, O = 16.00 g/mol, N = 14.01 g/mol, Na = 22.99 g/mol, Cl = 35.45 g/mol.

worked.title: Simple: moles of water from 3.00 mol H₂ (excess O₂)
steps: Given: 3.00 mol H₂. Oxygen is in excess, so H₂ limits the product.
Write the mole ratio that links H₂ to H₂O from the coefficients: (2 mol H₂O)/(2 mol H₂).
That ratio simplifies to (1 mol H₂O)/(1 mol H₂), but keep it clear: multiply by (2 mol H₂O)/(2 mol H₂).
Set up: 3.00 mol H₂ × (2 mol H₂O)/(2 mol H₂).
Sig figs: 3.00 has 3 sig figs. Coefficients are exact. Answer: 3.00 mol H₂O.

sections.heading: Grams to grams through moles
paragraphs: Lab balances read grams, not moles. So a full stoichiometry path is usually: grams of A → moles of A → moles of B → grams of B. The middle step uses the mole ratio from the balanced equation. The outer steps use molar masses.
Never multiply grams of A by a mole ratio as if grams were moles. That skips the conversion and gives a wrong size answer.

worked.title: Harder: mass of H₂O from 10.0 g H₂ with excess O₂
steps: Given mass: 10.0 g H₂. O₂ is excess.
Convert grams H₂ to moles H₂: 10.0 g H₂ × (1 mol H₂)/(2.016 g H₂).
Compute moles H₂: 10.0 / 2.016 = 4.960317... mol H₂. Keep extra digits for now: 4.960317 mol H₂.
Apply the mole ratio to water: 4.960317 mol H₂ × (2 mol H₂O)/(2 mol H₂).
Cancel mol H₂. Moles H₂O = 4.960317 mol H₂O.
Convert to grams: 4.960317 mol H₂O × (18.016 g H₂O)/(1 mol H₂O).
Sig figs: the given 10.0 g has 3 sig figs. Atomic masses used here are treated as at least as precise. Round the final mass to 3 sig figs.
89.365... rounds to 89.4 g because the digit after 3 is 6.

sections.heading: Limiting reactant and percent yield
paragraphs: When two reactants are both given in limited amounts, one will run out first. That reactant is the limiting reactant (limiting reagent). It caps how much product can form. The other reactant is in excess. Some of it will be left over.

How to find the limiting reactant: convert each given amount to moles of product using the mole ratios. The reactant that produces the smaller amount of product is limiting. Use only that smaller amount for later yield calculations.
Theoretical yield is the mass of product predicted by stoichiometry from the limiting reactant, assuming the reaction goes to completion with no losses.
Actual yield is the mass you obtain in the lab. It is almost always less than theoretical yield because of incomplete reaction, side reactions, or loss during transfer.
Percent yield = (actual yield / theoretical yield) × 100%. Both yields must use the same unit, usually grams.

worked.title: Limiting reactant: 5.00 g H₂ and 40.0 g O₂ making water
steps: Moles of H₂: 5.00 g × (1 mol / 2.016 g) = 2.48016 mol H₂.
Moles of O₂: molar mass O₂ = 32.00 g/mol. 40.0 g × (1 mol / 32.00 g) = 1.250 mol O₂.
Moles of H₂O from H₂ if H₂ is fully used: 2.48016 mol H₂ × (2 mol H₂O)/(2 mol H₂) = 2.48016 mol H₂O.
Moles of H₂O from O₂ if O₂ is fully used: 1.250 mol O₂ × (2 mol H₂O)/(1 mol O₂) = 2.500 mol H₂O.
Compare 2.48016 mol and 2.500 mol. The smaller is 2.48016 mol. So H₂ is limiting.
Round to 3 sig figs to match 5.00 g: 44.7 g H₂O theoretical.

workedExamples.title: Percent yield if the lab collects 40.0 g H₂O from the run above
steps: Theoretical yield from the previous example = 44.7 g.
Sig figs: 40.0 and 44.7 each have 3 sig figs. Report 3 sig figs in the percentage.

mistake.wrong: Common mistake: picking the limiting reactant as whichever reactant has the smaller mass in grams (here choosing H₂ only because 5.00 g < 40.0 g) without converting to moles of product.
mistake.whyWrong: Grams of different substances are not comparable as amounts of reaction. O₂ molecules are heavier than H₂ molecules. You must compare how much product each given amount can make, using moles and the balanced coefficients.
mistake.correct: Correct way: convert each reactant to moles of product. The smaller product amount wins. In the example, H₂ still was limiting, but that conclusion came from 2.48 mol H₂O vs 2.50 mol H₂O, not from comparing 5 g to 40 g.

sections.heading: Solution dilution
paragraphs: Concentration in many early problems is molarity. Molarity M = moles of solute / liters of solution. A 0.50 M NaCl solution has 0.50 mol NaCl in each 1.00 L of solution.

Dilution means adding solvent (usually water) to a concentrated stock solution. The number of moles of solute stays the same. Only the volume changes. That is why the dilution equation works: M₁V₁ = M₂V₂. The product M×V is proportional to moles when volume is in liters (or when both volumes use the same unit).
M₁ and V₁ are the molarity and volume of the stock piece you measure out. M₂ and V₂ are the molarity and volume of the diluted solution after you add solvent and mix.

worked.title: Prepare 250. mL of 0.100 M HCl from 1.00 M HCl stock
steps: Identify: M₁ = 1.00 M (stock), M₂ = 0.100 M (diluted), V₂ = 250. mL.
Keep volume units consistent. Convert V₂ to liters: 250. mL × (1 L)/(1000 mL) = 0.250 L.
Write M₁V₁ = M₂V₂ and solve for V₁: V₁ = (M₂V₂)/M₁.
Compute the numerator: 0.100 × 0.250 = 0.0250 mol (the moles of HCl needed).
Divide by M₁: 0.0250 mol / 1.00 mol/L = 0.0250 L.
Convert V₁ to mL if that is how you will pipette: 0.0250 L × 1000 mL/L = 25.0 mL.
Sig figs: 0.100, 250., and 1.00 each support 3 sig figs. Answer: measure 25.0 mL of 1.00 M HCl and add water until the total volume is 250. mL.

sections.heading: Check yourself
paragraphs: Try these, then reveal the answers.

items.q: In N₂ + 3 H₂ → 2 NH₃, how many moles of NH₃ form from 6.0 mol H₂ if N₂ is excess?
items.a: 6.0 mol H₂ × (2 mol NH₃)/(3 mol H₂) = 4.0 mol NH₃.

items.q: What is the molar mass of CO₂ using C = 12.01 and O = 16.00?
You need 500. mL of 0.200 M NaCl from 1.00 M stock. What volume of stock do you take?
items.a: V₁ = (0.200 × 0.500 L)/1.00 = 0.100 L = 100. mL of stock, then dilute to 500. mL.

sections.heading: Light as energy packets
paragraphs: Light is electromagnetic radiation. Frequency ν and wavelength λ are linked by c = λν, with c = 2.998 × 10⁸ m/s. Photon energy E = hν = hc/λ, where h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s.

sections.heading: The Bohr model for hydrogen
paragraphs: In hydrogen, electron energy levels are E_n = −13.6 eV / n². A jump from higher n to lower n emits a photon whose energy equals the level gap. The Balmer line n=3→2 is the famous red 656 nm line.

figure.alt: Bohr energy-level diagram for hydrogen showing n=1, 2, 3 and infinity, with a red emission arrow for the Balmer n=3 to n=2 photon at 656 nm.

sections.heading: Orbitals and quantum numbers
paragraphs: Quantum numbers label orbitals: n (shell), ℓ (subshell: s,p,d,f), m_ℓ (orientation), m_s (spin ±½). An orbital holds at most two electrons with opposite spins (Pauli principle).

figure.alt: Schematic orbital shapes: spherical 1s, dumbbell 2p with plus and minus lobes, and a four-leaf 3d clover (dx2−y2 style).

sections.heading: Building configurations
paragraphs: Fill orbitals in order of increasing energy (Aufbau): 1s → 2s → 2p → 3s → 3p → 4s → 3d → 4p … Hund's rule: put one electron in each degenerate orbital before pairing.
Noble-gas shorthand writes the previous noble gas in brackets, then the remaining valence configuration. The block of the periodic table (s, p, d, f) matches the last subshell filled.

figure.alt: Orbital box diagrams for carbon (1s2 2s2 2p2 with two unpaired 2p electrons) and nitrogen (1s2 2s2 2p3 with three unpaired 2p electrons) illustrating Hund’s rule.

worked.title: Find the element [Kr]4d¹⁰5s²5p³
steps: After Kr, add 4d¹⁰ 5s² 5p³ → total electrons beyond Kr: 15

sections.heading: Exceptions and ions
paragraphs: Cr and Cu prefer half-filled or filled d subshells: Cr is [Ar]3d⁵4s¹ (not 3d⁴4s²). For transition-metal cations, remove s electrons before d electrons: Fe is [Ar]3d⁶4s²; Fe³⁺ is [Ar]3d⁵.

figure.alt: Orbital box diagrams for chromium as [Ar] 3d5 4s1 with six unpaired electrons, and for Fe3+ as [Ar] 3d5 with five unpaired 3d electrons.

sections.heading: Atomic and ionic radius
paragraphs: Atomic radius generally decreases across a period (more protons pull the same shell tighter) and increases down a group (new shells). For isoelectronic ions (same electron count), more protons → smaller radius.

worked.title: Order Na⁺, Mg²⁺, F⁻, O²⁻ by increasing radius
steps: Nuclear charge: Mg 12 > Na 11 > F 9 > O 8
Higher Z pulls electrons closer → smaller ion

sections.heading: Ionization energy
paragraphs: First ionization energy (IE₁) generally rises across a period and falls down a group. Exceptions: Be→B and N→O. Removing a paired 2p electron from O is easier than removing an unpaired 2p electron from N because of electron–electron repulsion in the pair.

sections.heading: Paramagnetism
paragraphs: A species is paramagnetic if it has unpaired electrons. Ca ([Ar]4s²) and Zn²⁺ ([Ar]3d¹⁰) are diamagnetic; Fe²⁺ ([Ar]3d⁶) has unpaired electrons and is paramagnetic.

figure.alt: Orbital boxes showing Ca ([Ar] 4s2) and Zn2+ ([Ar] 3d10) with zero unpaired electrons (diamagnetic), and Fe2+ ([Ar] 3d6) with four unpaired electrons (paramagnetic).

sections.heading: Lewis structures
paragraphs: Count valence electrons, connect atoms with single bonds, complete octets (H wants 2), and use multiple bonds or formal charge to refine. Formal charge = valence − (nonbonding e⁻) − ½(bonding e⁻).

figure.alt: Lewis structures of H2O (bent, two lone pairs on oxygen), CO2 (linear O=C=O), and SF4 (sulfur with four F bonds and one lone pair); all formal charges zero.

sections.heading: VSEPR shapes and polarity
paragraphs: Electron domains (bonds + lone pairs) arrange to minimize repulsion. Domains: 2 linear, 3 trigonal planar, 4 tetrahedral, 5 trigonal bipyramidal, 6 octahedral. Lone pairs take equatorial sites in TBP when possible.
Molecular shape ignores lone pairs for the name but includes them for angles. A molecule is polar if bond dipoles do not cancel.

figure.alt: Three-dimensional seesaw shape of SF4 from trigonal bipyramidal electron geometry with an equatorial lone pair, and a net dipole arrow showing the molecule is polar.

worked.title: Shape and polarity of SF₄
steps: S has 6 valence e⁻; 4 F atoms → 4 bonds + 1 lone pair = 5 domains
Electron geometry: trigonal bipyramidal; molecular shape: seesaw
Lone pair and unsymmetric shape → dipoles do not cancel → polar

sections.heading: Bond enthalpies for reaction ΔH
paragraphs: Estimate ΔH ≈ Σ bonds broken − Σ bonds formed (using mean bond enthalpies). Breaking absorbs energy (+); forming releases (−).

worked.title: Estimate ΔH for H₂ + Cl₂ → 2 HCl
steps: Break 1 H–H and 1 Cl–Cl; form 2 H–Cl
Using typical mean values → about −184 kJ

sections.heading: Hybridization and σ / π bonds
paragraphs: Hybrid orbitals mix atomic orbitals to match the electron geometry: sp (linear), sp² (trigonal planar), sp³ (tetrahedral). A single bond is one σ bond. A double bond is σ + π; a triple is σ + 2π.

figure.alt: Hybridization sketch of ethene (sp2 carbons, one sigma and one pi bond) beside ethyne (sp carbons, one sigma and two pi bonds), with sigma in blue and pi in red.

worked.title: σ and π bonds in CH₂=CH–C≡N
steps: σ bonds: 4 C–H + C–C + C–N = 6 σ
Every connection has one σ (singles, doubles, and triples each include one)
Double bond adds 1 π; triple bond adds 2 π → 3 π total

sections.heading: Molecular orbital (MO) theory
paragraphs: Atomic orbitals combine into bonding and antibonding MOs. Bond order = ½(bonding e⁻ − antibonding e⁻). Higher bond order → shorter, stronger bond. O₂ has two unpaired electrons in π* orbitals, so it is paramagnetic — Lewis structures miss this.

figure.alt: Molecular orbital energy diagram for O2 with sigma 2p below pi 2p, two unpaired electrons in pi-star, bond order 2 and paramagnetism; notes compare O2+ (BO 2.5) and O2− (BO 1.5).

worked.title: Bond orders of O₂, O₂⁺, O₂⁻
steps: O₂ has 12 valence electrons in the MO scheme. Bond order = 2.
O₂⁺ removes one antibonding e⁻ → bond order 2.5
O₂⁻ adds one antibonding e⁻ → bond order 1.5

sections.heading: Types of intermolecular forces
paragraphs: London dispersion: instantaneous dipoles; stronger for larger, more polarizable electron clouds and for longer contact area. Dipole–dipole: between permanent dipoles. Hydrogen bonding: H bonded to N, O, or F attracted to a lone pair on N, O, or F. It is unusually strong.
Stronger IMF → higher boiling/melting point (for similar molar mass).

worked.title: Boiling points: HF, Ne, HCl
steps: Ne: only weak dispersion → lowest bp

sections.heading: Shape matters
paragraphs: Straight-chain alkanes have more surface contact than branched isomers, so stronger dispersion and higher boiling points. Pentane boils higher than neopentane.

figure.alt: Side-by-side carbon skeletons of straight-chain n-pentane and compact neopentane (2,2-dimethylpropane), noting that more surface contact raises boiling point via stronger London forces.

sections.heading: Clausius–Clapeyron
paragraphs: Vapor pressure rises with T. ln(P₂/P₁) = −(ΔH_vap/R)(1/T₂ − 1/T₁). Use absolute temperatures (K).

sections.heading: Gas laws and PV = nRT
paragraphs: Boyle: P ∝ 1/V at fixed n,T. Charles: V ∝ T (K). Avogadro: V ∝ n. Combined ideal-gas law: PV = nRT. Use consistent R (0.082057 L·atm·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹ when P in atm and V in L).

worked.title: P for 2.50 mol in 10.0 L at 25.0 °C

sections.heading: Molar mass and density
paragraphs: At the same T and P, equal volumes of ideal gases have equal moles (Avogadro). So denser gas = larger molar mass. CO₂ (44 g/mol) is denser than N₂ (28 g/mol) at the same T,P.

sections.heading: Partial pressures
paragraphs: Dalton's law: P_total = Σ P_i. Mole fraction x_i = n_i / n_total; P_i = x_i P_total.

sections.heading: Kinetic-molecular ideas
paragraphs: Gas pressure comes from collisions with the walls. Average translational KE per mole = (3/2)RT. Root-mean-square speed u_rms = √(3RT/M) with M in kg/mol.

sections.heading: Effusion and diffusion (Graham)
paragraphs: Rate of effusion ∝ 1/√M. Ratio of rates = √(M_heavy / M_light).

sections.heading: Real gases
paragraphs: Ideal gas ignores volume of molecules and attractions. At high P or low T, use van der Waals: (P + a n²/V²)(V − n b) = nRT. a corrects attractions; b corrects volume.

sections.heading: First law: ΔU = q + w
paragraphs: Internal energy U is a state function. Heat q into the system is positive; work w done on the system is positive in the chemistry sign convention used here (some physics books define w with the opposite sign). For expansion work against constant P, w = −PΔV.

worked.title: System absorbs 250 J heat, does 100 J work
steps: w = −100 J (system does work on surroundings)

sections.heading: Enthalpy and calorimetry
paragraphs: H = U + PV. At constant pressure, q_p = ΔH. Coffee-cup calorimetry: q_sol ≈ −m c ΔT for the solution (sign flips for the reaction).

sections.heading: Hess's law and ΔH_f°
paragraphs: ΔH°_rxn = Σ n ΔH_f°(products) − Σ n ΔH_f°(reactants). Elements in standard state have ΔH_f° = 0.

worked.title: ΔH° for CH₄ + 2 O₂ → CO₂ + 2 H₂O(l)

sections.heading: K and Q
paragraphs: For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD, K_c = [C]^c[D]^d / ([A]^a[B]^b) at equilibrium. Q uses the same form with current concentrations. If Q < K, forward; Q > K, reverse; Q = K, at equilibrium.
K_p uses partial pressures in bar (or atm when that is the standard). K_p = K_c (RT)^{Δn} with Δn = moles gas products − reactants, and R = 0.082057 L·atm·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹ when pressures are in atm.

worked.title: K_p from K_c for N₂ + 3 H₂ ⇌ 2 NH₃

sections.heading: ICE tables
paragraphs: Set Initial amounts, define Change with x using stoichiometry, write Equilibrium expressions, solve using K.

worked.title: H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2 HI, K=49.0, start 0.0100 M each

sections.heading: Entropy
paragraphs: Entropy S measures dispersal of energy / number of microstates. Gases have much higher S than liquids or solids. Fewer gas moles → usually ΔS < 0. Standard entropy change: ΔS° = Σ n S°(products) − Σ n S°(reactants).

worked.title: Sign of ΔS for 2 H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2 H₂O(l)

sections.heading: Gibbs energy
paragraphs: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS (T in kelvin). Spontaneous as written when ΔG < 0. ΔG° = −RT ln K links thermodynamics to equilibrium. When ΔH > 0 and ΔS > 0, the reaction becomes spontaneous above T = ΔH/ΔS.

sections.heading: Rate laws and order
paragraphs: Rate = k [A]^m [B]^n … Orders m,n are found experimentally, not from stoichiometry. First-order: ln[A] = ln[A]₀ − kt; half-life t½ = ln 2 / k (constant).

sections.heading: Integrated first-order use
paragraphs: [A] = [A]₀ e^{−kt}. Plug in k and t to find remaining concentration.

sections.heading: Arrhenius equation
paragraphs: k = A e^{−Ea/RT}. From two temperatures: ln(k₂/k₁) = −(Ea/R)(1/T₂ − 1/T₁).

worked.title: Ea when k doubles from 300 K to 310 K

sections.heading: Brønsted–Lowry and conjugates
paragraphs: Acid donates H⁺; base accepts H⁺. After transfer, the acid becomes its conjugate base and the base becomes its conjugate acid. Water can act as either (amphoteric).

worked.title: Conjugate pairs in NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻

sections.heading: Strong acids and pH
paragraphs: Strong acids (HCl, HBr, HI, HNO₃, H₂SO₄ first proton, HClO₄) dissociate fully. For dilute strong monoprotic acid, [H₃O⁺] ≈ C_a; pH = −log[H₃O⁺].

sections.heading: Weak acids
paragraphs: For HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻, K_a = [H⁺][A⁻]/[HA]. If x ≪ C_a, [H⁺] ≈ √(K_a C_a). Acetic acid K_a ≈ 1.8×10⁻⁵ (standard value; confirm against your table).

sections.heading: Buffers and Henderson–Hasselbalch
paragraphs: A buffer is a weak acid + its conjugate base (or weak base + conjugate acid). pH ≈ pK_a + log([A⁻]/[HA]). Best buffering when [A⁻]≈[HA] and both are reasonably concentrated.

sections.heading: Adding strong base to a buffer
paragraphs: OH⁻ converts HA → A⁻. Update the mole amounts, then reapply Henderson–Hasselbalch.

sections.heading: Equivalence point
paragraphs: For weak acid + strong base, the salt at equivalence is a weak base (A⁻), so pH > 7. Solve from K_b = K_w/K_a and the A⁻ concentration after dilution.

sections.heading: Electrolytes
paragraphs: Strong electrolytes dissociate fully (strong acids, strong soluble bases, soluble ionic salts). Weak electrolytes partially dissociate (weak acids/bases). Non-electrolytes (e.g. glucose, ethanol) dissolve as molecules.

sections.heading: Precipitation and net ionic equations
paragraphs: Write the full molecular equation, then the complete ionic equation, then cancel spectator ions to get the net ionic equation. Solubility rules decide which salts precipitate.

worked.title: AgNO₃(aq) + NaCl(aq)
steps: Ionic: Ag⁺ + NO₃⁻ + Na⁺ + Cl⁻ → AgCl(s) + Na⁺ + NO₃⁻

sections.heading: Redox in solution
paragraphs: Oxidation is loss of electrons; reduction is gain. The oxidizing agent is reduced; the reducing agent is oxidized. In Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, Cu²⁺ is the oxidizing agent and Zn is the reducing agent.

figure.alt: Simple redox sketch: zinc metal donates two electrons to aqueous Cu2+, labeling Zn as the reducing agent (oxidized) and Cu2+ as the oxidizing agent (reduced).

sections.heading: K_sp
paragraphs: For M_mX_x(s) ⇌ m Mⁿ⁺ + x Xʸ⁻, K_sp = [M]^m [X]^x. Molar solubility s is the moles of solid that dissolve per litre.

worked.title: K_sp of CaF₂ from s = 2.1×10⁻⁴ M

sections.heading: Will it precipitate?
paragraphs: Compute Q with the mixed ion concentrations (after dilution). If Q > K_sp, precipitate forms; Q < K_sp, no precipitate; Q = K_sp, saturated.

worked.title: PbCl₂ after mixing
steps: Compare to K_sp(PbCl₂); Q < K_sp → no precipitate

sections.heading: Complex ions
paragraphs: Metal ions can bind ligands (NH₃, OH⁻, CN⁻…) to form complex ions, which can raise the apparent solubility of a precipitate (e.g. AgCl in NH₃).

figure.alt: Linear [Ag(NH3)2]+ complex with silver at the center and two ammine ligands, overall charge +1, coordination number 2.

sections.heading: Half-reaction method (acidic)
paragraphs: Split into oxidation and reduction half-reactions. Balance atoms other than O and H, then O with H₂O, then H with H⁺, then charge with e⁻. Multiply to equalize electrons and add.

worked.title: MnO₄⁻ + Fe²⁺ → Mn²⁺ + Fe³⁺ (acidic)
steps: Reduction: MnO₄⁻ → Mn²⁺; add 4 H₂O, 8 H⁺, 5 e⁻
Add: MnO₄⁻ + 5 Fe²⁺ + 8 H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5 Fe³⁺ + 4 H₂O

sections.heading: Basic solution
paragraphs: Balance as if acidic, then add OH⁻ to both sides to neutralize H⁺, forming water, and cancel extra H₂O.

worked.title: MnO₄⁻ + I⁻ → MnO₂ + I₂ (basic)
steps: Acidic balance first, then convert H⁺ to H₂O with OH⁻
Result: 2 MnO₄⁻ + 6 I⁻ + 4 H₂O → 2 MnO₂ + 3 I₂ + 8 OH⁻

sections.heading: Redox titration
paragraphs: Use the balanced electron ratio to relate moles of titrant to analyte. Example: 1 MnO₄⁻ oxidizes 5 Fe²⁺ in acid.

sections.heading: Galvanic cells
paragraphs: A galvanic (voltaic) cell runs a spontaneous redox reaction to make electric current. Oxidation at the anode; reduction at the cathode. E°_cell = E°_cathode − E°_anode (using reduction potentials).

figure.alt: Galvanic cell Zn|Zn2+||Cu2+|Cu with zinc anode (oxidation), copper cathode (reduction), salt bridge, electron flow through the wire toward copper, and E° cell = 1.10 V.

worked.title: E° for Zn–Cu cell
steps: E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V; E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = −0.76 V (standard table values)

sections.heading: ΔG°, K, and E°
paragraphs: ΔG° = −n F E°_cell. Positive E°_cell means ΔG° < 0 and K > 1 (products favored at standard state).

sections.heading: Nernst equation
paragraphs: At 25 °C: E = E° − (0.0592/n) log Q. Lower [product ions] / higher [reactant ions] raises E for the forward cell reaction.

sections.heading: Absorption and energy
paragraphs: Molecules absorb photons that match an allowed energy gap. E = hc/λ per photon; multiply by N_A for per-mole energy. Longer λ → smaller energy.

sections.heading: IR and wavenumbers
paragraphs: Infrared often reported as wavenumber ν̃ = 1/λ (cm⁻¹). Bond vibrations: stronger/lighter bonds → higher wavenumber.

sections.heading: Conjugation and color
paragraphs: In conjugated π systems, the HOMO–LUMO gap shrinks as the chain lengthens, so λ_max moves to longer wavelength (bathochromic shift). Enough conjugation and the absorption enters the visible — the compound looks colored.

figure.alt: Qualitative HOMO–LUMO gaps for ethene, butadiene, and hexatriene showing the gap shrinking as conjugation lengthens, which shifts absorption to longer wavelength.
